title: Find the Celebrity
statement:
There are `n` people at a party, labeled `0` to `n - 1`. A **celebrity** is a person whom all of the other `n - 1` people know, while the celebrity knows none of them. Knowing goes one way: `a` may know `b` even though `b` does not know `a`. Return the label of the celebrity, or `-1` when nobody at the party is one (two celebrities can never exist at once).

You cannot look at the relationships directly. Your function is called as `findCelebrity(n)`, and it may call the global helper `knows(a, b)`, which returns `true` exactly when person `a` knows person `b`. Use as few calls as you can: O(n) calls are enough, and a follow-up asks you to stay within `3 * n` of them.

Each case is written as `[graph]`: an `n` by `n` matrix in which `graph[a][b] == 1` means `a` knows `b`, and every person knows themselves (`graph[i][i] == 1`). The matrix is only answered through `knows`; it is not passed to your function.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking each person against everyone else answers the question with O(n²) calls to `knows`. Every single call, though, rules somebody out. If `a` knows `b`, then `a` knows someone and cannot be the celebrity; if `a` does not know `b`, then `b` is unknown to someone and cannot be the celebrity either. So one pass that keeps a single surviving candidate eliminates everyone else in `n - 1` calls. The survivor is the only possible celebrity, but it still has to be checked, because maybe nobody qualifies.

## Approach

1. Start with `candidate = 0`.
2. For each `i` from 1 to `n - 1`, ask `knows(candidate, i)`. If it is true, the current candidate is out and `i` becomes the new `candidate`; otherwise `i` is out.
3. Verify the survivor: for every other person `i`, the candidate must not know `i`, and `i` must know the candidate. Any failure means there is no celebrity, so return `-1`.
4. If every check passes, return `candidate`.

## Example 1, step by step

`graph = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]]`, so `n = 3`.

- `candidate = 0`. `knows(0, 1)` is true, so `candidate = 1`.
- `knows(1, 2)` is false, so person 2 is ruled out and `candidate` stays 1.
- Check `i = 0`: `knows(1, 0)` is false and `knows(0, 1)` is true. Skip `i = 1`. Check `i = 2`: `knows(1, 2)` is false and `knows(2, 1)` is true.

All checks pass, so the answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), with at most `3 * (n - 1)` calls to `knows`: `n - 1` in the first pass and two per other person in the check.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The first pass only proves that nobody **else** can be the celebrity; returning `candidate` without the check fails parties that have no celebrity.
- The check must test both directions: the candidate knows nobody, and everybody knows the candidate.
- Skip `i === candidate` in the check, since everyone knows themselves and `knows(candidate, candidate)` is true.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of people at the party |
| `candidate` | the only person not yet ruled out |
| `i` | the person being compared with the candidate |

narration.2: Person 0 is the first candidate; nobody has been ruled out yet.
narration.3: Compare the candidate with each of the remaining people once.
narration.4: If the candidate knows i, the candidate cannot be the celebrity.
narration.5: So i takes over as the candidate; otherwise i is the one ruled out.
narration.9: The survivor is the only possible celebrity; check it against everyone.
narration.10: Everyone knows themselves, so the candidate is not compared with itself.
narration.13: The candidate knowing someone, or someone not knowing the candidate, breaks the definition.
narration.14: So the party has no celebrity.
narration.17: Every check passed: the candidate is the celebrity.
